open_questions: Is the ~11050 ppm dip near phase 0.7512 (secondary snr 5.297, secondary_over_bump 1.612, phase_curve chi2 30.53 dof 7) a true secondary eclipse of an EB or ellipsoidal/spot modulation aliased by the 14.7 d period? High-precision follow-up and radial velocities needed.
Why is fit_b 0.9866 (extremely grazing) required? RV and follow-up transit shape will check stellar density (fit_log_density_ratio -2.368) mismatch.
dossier.public_summary: TESS shows a 14.7-day dip about 1% deep around a nearby M dwarf in three consistent sectors, implying a 2.5 Earth-radius planet. The boxy, grazing shape and a marginal dip near half-orbit overlap binary signs, but there is no neighbour that can mimic it and the individual transits agree, so a planet is still the best explanation. A follow-up observation to refine the transit shape and test the marginal secondary signal will confirm whether the boxy shape is grazing or binary.

reasons.why: Planet-sized transit; well below giant-planet/star limit despite 15% phase-curve amplitude. Photometric M dwarf (teff 3276, rad 0.2213) implied radius is 2.53 R_earth.
Three transits are individually consistent with one mean depth (10863 ppm); signal is not driven by one odd outlier transit.
Depth is stable across three sectors despite different apertures and pointing, positive evidence against a blend whose depth should change with aperture and against noise.

No star within one TESS pixel (21 arcsec) can produce the 10940 ppm dip even with a total eclipse; the plausible eclipsing-binary scenario would require a background source at ~67 arcsec with very deep eclipse, disfavored by stable depth and rule-out of on-target neighbours.

Formally ~5.3 sigma secondary near phase 0.7512 is equally deep as primary, the classic signature of a stellar eclipse (not a tiny hot-Jupiter occultation), but it is just above detection and coincident with a high phase-curve (amplitude_ppm 1603 ratio_to_depth 0.1465 chi2 30.53 dof 7) that is expected from this star's rapid rotation (fit_b 0.9866 grazing geometry). Gaia EB target_match null and no RUWE anomaly do not confirm it, and the scorer's low xgboost planet_rank 0.07 reflects this boxy, grazing shape rather than a third transit; additional high-precision photometry can test but does not outweigh planet-size, stable multi-sector consistency and lack of blend.
